l: the nobility of man, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: The nobility of man is an office-based nobility including gong, qing, and da fu; it may follow cultivating Heaven’s nobility, but pursuing it while discarding the higher nobility is extreme delusion.
Water subdues fire as benevolence, yet one cup cannot save burning fuel; under Yu's regulation, it flows into four seas.
Life is valued but less than righteousness; amid sorrow and calamity, people should not preserve it through improper means or prefer it to death.
Death is disliked, yet people may accept danger rather than violate righteousness, showing that life is not the highest value.

Men commonly desire honour, yet possess truly honourable qualities without recognizing them. When satiated with benevolence and righteousness, they cease desiring conferred honours, fat meat, fine millet, and elegant embroidered garments.
Honour humanly conferred is unstable and not good; true honour, unlike status men can grant or revoke, is associated with benevolence and righteousness.
Fire represents the force opposed to benevolence. A whole wagon-load of burning fuel cannot be extinguished by only one cup of water.
teaches shooting [by drawing the bow to the full] Yi teaches men to shoot by drawing the bow to the full. His pupils follow the same rule.

l: rules of propriety, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: Rules of propriety are said to outweigh eating and sexual appetite, but Mencius says their importance depends on the competing matter and circumstance.
Filial piety and fraternal duty are described as the simple course followed by Yao and Shun. Confucius is cited as saying that Shun remained full of longing desire about his parents even at fifty.

undermines benevolence and righteousness [when made the basis of social relations] Mencius rejects profit as the foundation for relations between rulers, ministers, fathers, sons, and brothers. He warns that serving a ruler by enriching him when the ruler lacks benevolence is to enrich a Jie.

l: benevolence and righteousness, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: supports royal sway [when made the basis of government] Mencius says that counsel based on benevolence and righteousness could lead rulers to stop warfare and cause ministers and families to act according to those principles. He contrasts this with relations governed by profit and says a state guided by benevolence and righteousness can rise to royal sway.

l: five chiefs of the princes, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: are_sinners_against three kings [for dragging princes to punish other princes] The five chiefs of the princes are described as sinners against the three kings because they dragged princes to punish other princes. The most powerful chief, the duke Huan, established prohibitions concerning filial conduct, worthy officials, the old and young, offices, grain, embankments, and announcements to the sovereign.
Princes are expected to serve the sovereign, cultivate territories, honor worthies, and appoint talent; present-day princes violate five prohibitions and are called sinners against five chiefs.

are_sinners_against princes [for anticipating and exciting their sovereigns' wickedness] The Great officers of the present day are called sinners against the princes because they anticipate and encourage their sovereigns' wickedness. Mencius distinguishes this from merely conniving at or aiding such wickedness, which he calls a smaller crime.

l: prince of Lu, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi)
s: The prince of Lu considers appointing Shen army commander and entrusting Lu’s administration to Yue Zheng; Mencius opposes war with an uninstructed people but welcomes Yue Zheng’s love of good.

Lu is a five-hundred-li-square territory, including Nan Yang as potentially taken from Qi; though larger than Zhou Gong’s original grant, it should be governed through benevolence and perhaps diminished by a true royal ruler.

Taxation is a revenue system proposed at one-twentieth of produce. Bai Gui advocates that rate; Mencius says it suits Mo but not the Middle Kingdom, which needs fuller institutions and Yao and Shun’s arrangements.

loves good [as his principal qualification] Yue Zheng is described as lacking vigour, wisdom in council, and extensive information, but as loving what is good. Mencius says this quality is more than sufficient for governing Lu because it attracts good men and keeps calumniators, flatterers, and sycophants from dominating the government.

qualifies_for government of the kingdom [when loved by a minister] Love of what is good is presented as a decisive qualification for government. Mencius says that a minister who loves what is good attracts good thoughts from far away, while self-conceit drives good men away and allows calumniators, flatterers, and sycophants to appear.

carries_into_practice words [when receiving a superior man into office] A prince may receive a superior man with great respect, but the man may leave if the prince does not act on his words or later becomes less polite. A prince who cannot follow a man’s doctrines may offer him only enough assistance to prevent death.

Superior men accept office under different conditions involving a prince’s respect and willingness to practice their teachings. Heaven may confer a great office on someone after subjecting him to suffering, toil, hunger, poverty, and frustrated plans.
has arts [many] Teaching is described as having many forms. Refusing to teach a man may nevertheless teach him.

This document is a collection of teachings attributed to Mencius, arranged in two parts, concerning self-cultivation, Heaven’s appointment, moral character, teaching, and benevolent government. Part I begins with the individual: people should know and preserve their Heaven-given nature, accept what is properly appointed, seek inward goods through effort, examine themselves for sincerity, and cultivate shame as a means of correction. Mencius contrasts habitual, unreflective living with the deliberate pursuit of virtue and righteousness. He describes the superior person and distinguished scholar as self-motivated, principled in poverty or prosperity, unimpressed by power or office, and devoted to rectifying themselves. Important examples include Shun, whose eager response to goodness distinguishes him even in remote surroundings; Yao and Shun, for whom benevolence and righteousness were natural; Tang and Wu, who made those principles their own; Hui of Liu Xia, who would not trade purpose for office; and Confucius, whose perspective and progressive learning exemplify the sage’s path. Mencius repeatedly connects moral cultivation to public life. Good rulers secure the people’s ease, prosperity, and virtue through instruction, light burdens, cultivated fields, care for the old, and abundant food. True sovereigns influence people deeply and almost imperceptibly, unlike mere chiefs. Good instruction gains hearts, whereas government gains wealth and fear. He presents king Wen’s care for the old and families as a model, and condemns unjust action, rigid principle detached from circumstances, and pursuit of gain over virtue. Dialogue chapters apply these standards to political and personal cases: Yi Yin may banish Tai Jia only if sharing his proper purpose; Shun would allow Gao Yao to arrest Gu Sou but would abandon the kingdom to care for his father; and scholars deserve genuine honor rather than empty gifts. Mencius defines teaching as varied influence, talent-development, answering inquiry, and prompting self-cultivation, while refusing to lower standards for incapable learners. Part II continues these concerns in summary form, treating benevolent rule, unjust war, the relations among people, sovereigns, government, sages, natural desire, Heaven’s appointment, and Confucius as a model and transmitter of earlier doctrines.

Mencius is a speaker and scholar whose teachings center on human nature, Heaven, shame, benevolence, righteousness, self-cultivation, and proper rule. He begins by connecting the full use of one’s mental constitution with knowing one’s nature and Heaven, while accepting what may rightly be called Heaven’s appointment. He teaches that all things are complete in us, that sincerity tested by self-examination is a great delight, and that reciprocity leads toward perfect virtue. Shame is indispensable: recognizing prior shamelessness can prevent its return. He contrasts habitual, unexamined conduct with the deliberate pursuit of the proper path. His account of character emphasizes innate moral capacities, intuitive knowledge, love for parents and elder brothers, and refusal to do or desire what righteousness forbids. Benevolence and righteousness distinguish humanity, while scholars should preserve their principles in either poverty or prosperity. He portrays superior people as independent of power, territory, population, and reputation, and as able to teach, counsel, transform society, and draw others toward the proper path. Mencius also sets standards for government. A true sovereign makes people deeply content; good government secures ease, preserves life, cultivates fields, lightens taxes, uses resources seasonably, and nourishes the old. He condemns unjust war, excessive taxation, false virtue, uncontrolled desires, and neglect of self-cultivation. Political action must remain subject to righteousness: even banishing a sovereign is usurpation unless it has the same purpose as Yi Yin. Across the chapters, his teaching moves from inner nature and moral discipline to the conduct of scholars, rulers, and society. It closes by presenting benevolence as extending care beyond what one initially values and by reaffirming the superior man’s responsibility to cultivate himself and guide others.

Heaven is known by knowing and nourishing one’s nature. It appoints events that may properly be ascribed to it, is associated with its people, and determinately apportions what belongs by nature to the superior man.

l: mental constitution, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: A person who exhausts their mental constitution knows their nature. Preserving it is part of the way to serve Heaven.

l: Heaven-conferred nature, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Knowing one's nature leads to knowing Heaven. Nourishing one's nature is part of the way to serve Heaven. Heaven-conferred nature includes the bodily organs and their functions.

l: the way, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The way preserves mental constitution, nourishes nature, cultivates character, and serves Heaven without distraction by death or longevity.

l: the appointment of Heaven, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Heaven's appointment is said to exist for everything and to be received submissively when correctly ascribed. It includes natural human feelings tied to bodily desires and righteousness in moral relations. The account links it to ordinary pleasures and prudence, while distinguishing moral conduct from natural desires.
Death sustained in duties may be ascribed to Heaven's appointment, while death under handcuffs and fetters cannot be so ascribed.

Seeking helps people obtain things within themselves when effort brings gain and neglect brings loss. It does not help obtain things outside themselves when seeking follows the proper course but what is gained is only as appointed.
Getting is gained through proper seeking in one case, but in another occurs only as an appointed outcome and cannot be produced by seeking.

l: the path of duty, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: A prosperous scholar does not leave the proper path. By remaining on it, the scholar does not disappoint the expectations of the people.

l: things sought for within ourselves, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: These are the things sought when seeking is useful to getting and people gain through seeking.

l: things sought outside ourselves, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: These are the things sought when seeking follows the proper course but getting is only as appointed.

l: all things, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: is_complete complete [in us] All things are said to be already complete in us.
is_examined self-examination [consciously] Sincerity becomes a source of the greatest delight when one is conscious of it through self-examination.

l: law of reciprocity, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: is_followed vigorous effort [at the law of reciprocity] The law of reciprocity is to be practiced with vigorous effort. Such effort brings one closest to perfect virtue when seeking its realization.

l: perfect virtue, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Perfect virtue is something one seeks to realize. Vigorous effort at the law of reciprocity is described as the closest approximation to it.
The multitudes follow the proper path throughout life without understanding or examining what they do.

l: way of multitudes, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The way of multitudes is habitual, unexamined action along the proper path without understanding its nature, followed throughout life.
A man may not lack shame; if ashamed of once lacking it, he thereafter has no occasion for further shame.
Shame may be absent from a man, but recognizing and feeling ashamed of that absence can prevent future occasions for shame.

l: sense of shame, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Sense of shame is very important to man, yet artful people prevent it from acting; some men lack it unlike others.

l: able and virtuous monarchs of antiquity, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: A group of able, virtuous antiquity monarchs loved virtue and forgot their power.
Virtue, loved by able and virtuous monarchs, is expected among well-provisioned people and earnestly practiced from cock-crowing rather than pursuing gain.
The able and virtuous monarchs of antiquity forgot their power. The power of princes was disregarded by the able and virtuous scholars of antiquity.

l: able and virtuous scholars of antiquity, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The able and virtuous scholars of antiquity delighted in their own principles, ignored princely power, and required kings and dukes to show utmost respect and ceremony before frequent visits.

l: kings and dukes, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Kings and dukes must show utmost respect and observe every ceremony when visiting able and virtuous scholars of antiquity; without frequent visits, they are even less permitted to employ those scholars as ministers.

l: Song Gou Jian, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Song Gou Jian asks Mencius what is required to secure perfect satisfaction. He is advised to honor virtue and delight in righteousness.
A scholar keeps righteousness in poverty and the proper path in prosperity, thereby possessing himself and meeting the people’s expectations.

l: men of antiquity, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Men of antiquity conferred benefits on the people when their wishes were realized; when not, they cultivated personal character, attended to virtue in poverty and solitude, and became illustrious, later advancing to dignity in prosperity.
The people receive benefits when the men of antiquity realize their wishes. Their expectations are not disappointed when a prosperous scholar does not leave the proper path.

l: perfect satisfaction, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Perfect satisfaction is secured through virtue and righteousness, and remains maintained whether a prince follows one’s counsels or different courts do not.

Virtue is equipment whose completeness withstands a corrupt age. Honored and delighted in, it secures perfect satisfaction through cultivation of personal character; it is weakened by conduct only resembling sincerity, purity, or disinterestedness, requiring true standards to expose corrupt appearances.

Righteousness is a natural quality of the superior man, rooted in the heart and expressed throughout the body. It opposes taking what one has no right to and is presented as the path of life. A poor scholar must not abandon it, since it supports perfect satisfaction, and it works through respect for elders. It begins in natural feelings that refuse wrongdoing, then unfolds by extending those feelings into sincere speech and action, proper conduct, and rejection of gain by guile. Declining a dish of rice, a plate of soup, or the kingdom of Qi may show righteousness, though these are small forms beside other moral obligations.
The kingdom becomes virtuous when men of antiquity gain dignity, may benefit from costly self-sacrifice, and is a place where right principles can either prevail throughout or disappear.

l: king Wen, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: King Wen, chief of the West, nourishes old people through agricultural and household regulations; this care gives the mass of men a rousing impulse as they await him.

l: mass of men, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: A mass of men waits for king Wen, then receives a rousing impulse.

l: scholars distinguished from the mass, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: rouses_itself self [without a king Wan] Scholars distinguished from the mass rouse themselves without a king Wan.
A man is given the families of Han and Wei. If he then looks upon himself without elation, he is far beyond the mass of men.

l: families of Han and Wei, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Families of Han and Wei, introduced in Chapter 11, test whether a man becomes elated upon looking at himself.

l: the peasantry, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The people are employed to secure their ease and, though toiled, do not murmur. They are also put to death to preserve their lives and, though they die, do not murmur at the person who kills them.

l: the people, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The people are the most important element in a nation and can make a sovereign by being gained. They become rich through well-cultivated fields and light taxes, and virtuous when pulse and grain are abundant. They suffer under multiple exactions, but welcome benevolent correction, as shown by their pleasure at Tai Jia’s banishment and return after he became virtuous.

l: putting the people to death, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: causes death of the people Putting the people to death is described as a way intended to preserve their lives. The people will not murmur at him who puts them to death.

l: death of the people, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The death of the people occurs when they are put to death in a way intended to preserve their lives. Though they die, they will not murmur at him who puts them to death.
leads princes [as a chief] The chief leads all the princes, under whom the people look brisk and cheerful.

A group of people appears brisk and cheerful under a chief. Under a true sovereign, it becomes deeply content, neither murmuring when slain nor crediting benefits to him, and gradually progresses toward goodness without knowing who guides it.

l: true sovereign, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The true sovereign brings deep contentment: people neither murmur when slain nor credit him when benefited.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The superior man is a person whose presence transforms and spiritually influences others toward goodness, often without their knowing the cause. He mends society and, while residing in a country, guides its sovereign toward tranquillity, wealth, and glory; his instruction also shapes the young into filial, obedient, true-hearted, and faithful people. His three delights are family security, freedom from shame before Heaven and people, and finding, teaching, and nourishing talented individuals. Though he may desire wide territory, numerous people, and the ability to tranquillize those within the four seas, his highest enjoyment lies in qualities rooted in his own nature, which endure in poverty and retirement and manifest throughout his body. He has counsels, does not eat the bread of idleness, and cannot be retained through empty demonstrations of respect. His teaching unfolds in five ways: timely influence, perfecting virtue, developing talents, answering inquiries, and encouraging private cultivation and correction. Finally, he models the path: drawing the bow without discharging the arrow, seeming to leap with it toward the mark, standing exactly in the middle for those able to follow.
The superior man’s influence is spiritual in nature, flowing abroad above and beneath like Heaven and Earth.
Heaven is used as a comparison for the broad, flowing influence of the superior man.
Earth is used as a comparison for the broad, flowing influence of the superior man.

l: kindly words, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: enter_less_deeply_into people [than reputation for kindness] Kindly words do not enter so deeply into men as a reputation for kindness.

l: reputation for kindness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: A reputation for kindness enters more deeply into men than kindly words.

l: good government, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Good government is feared by people and gets their wealth, while good instructions burden people less.
The people fear good government yet love good instructions, giving wealth to government and hearts to instructions.

l: good instructions, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Good instructions, loved by people and winning their hearts, hold them more strongly than good government.
Wealth should be expended only on prescribed ceremonies; when food is used seasonably and wealth is properly spent, it exceeds consumption.

l: intuitive ability, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: is_a ability Intuitive ability is the ability possessed by men without having been acquired by learning.

l: intuitive knowledge, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: is_a knowledge Intuitive knowledge is the knowledge possessed by men without the exercise of thought.
Children learn to love their parents when carried in the arms, then love their elder brothers as they grow a little.

l: parents (children's parents), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Children naturally know to love their parents.

l: elder brothers (children's elder brothers), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: When children are grown a little, they naturally know to love their elder brothers.

l: filial affection, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Filial affection for parents is a working of benevolence, belonging to all under heaven.

Benevolence is a quality natural to the superior man, rooted in the heart and expressed in harmonious bearing and ordered conduct. It is the heart’s dwelling-place, rejects killing even one innocent person, and begins through filial affection for parents. It does not require kindness to every man, but includes cultivating affection for the virtuous. As man’s distinguishing characteristic, it arises by extending reluctance to injure others; embodied in conduct, it is called the path of duty. A benevolent ruler has no enemy under heaven.

l: respect for elders, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Respect for elders is the working of righteousness and belongs to all under heaven.

l: all under heaven, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The feelings of filial affection for parents and respect for elders belong to all under heaven.

Shun is a sovereign whose natural benevolence and righteousness guide a life of earnest attention to virtue and what is important. In retirement he lives amid mountains, trees, rocks, deer, and swine, seeming little different from remote-hill inhabitants, yet responds irresistibly to even one good word or action. His wisdom does not extend to everything, but he concentrates on what matters. Faced with Gu Sou’s apprehension, he would not interfere; he would abandon the kingdom like a worn-out sandal, carry Gu Sou into concealment by the sea, forget the kingdom, and live there cheerfully for life.

l: good word, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: A single good word causes Shun to respond with an irresistible flood of enthusiasm.

l: good action, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: A single good action causes Shun to respond with an irresistible flood of enthusiasm.
A man follows his sense of righteousness, refraining from actions and desires it rejects; Chapter 17 presents this guidance as all he has to do.

l: sense of righteousness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: tells man [what not to do and not to desire] The sense of righteousness tells a man what not to do and what not to desire. Following its guidance is described as sufficient for the man.

l: men (Mencius's statement), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Men with intelligent virtue and prudence, including friendless ministers and concubines’ sons, gain intelligence through sickness, troubles, and precautions against calamity.

l: sickness and troubles, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Sickness and troubles are associated with men who become intelligent in virtue and prudent in affairs.

l: friendless minister, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The friendless minister, alert to peril and calamity, becomes distinguished for intelligence through deep precautions.

l: concubine's son, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The concubine's son, mindful of peril and precautions against calamity, becomes distinguished for intelligence.
The friendless minister and the concubine's son use deep precautions against calamity.
Intelligence is associated with men who have experienced sickness and troubles and who remain cautious under a sense of peril. Such men become distinguished for their intelligence.

l: persons who serve the prince, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Persons serve the prince for the sake of his countenance and favour.

l: prince (persons who serve the prince), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The prince is served by persons who seek his countenance and favour.

l: ministers who seek the tranquillity of the State, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Ministers seek the State’s tranquillity and find pleasure in securing it.
The State is an object of tranquillity sought and secured by certain ministers.

l: people of Heaven, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: People of Heaven believe office would let them carry out principles throughout the kingdom, then proceed to do so.

l: great men, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Great men rectify themselves first, and through this others are rectified.
Tranquillity is sought for the State and is secured by ministers who take pleasure in securing it.
The people of Heaven believe they could carry out their principles throughout the kingdom if they were in office.

The kingdom is the realm where Heaven’s people carry out their principles. It should be ruled by a sage or prince who nourishes the old, makes pulse and grain abundant, and fosters virtue. Yet Shun would discard and forget it, living cheerfully in concealment by the sea-coast.

l: three delights, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The three delights are family well-being, freedom from shame before Heaven and people, and teaching and nourishing the kingdom's most talented individuals. Ruling the kingdom is excluded from the three delights.

l: the superior man's nature, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The superior man's nature is Heaven-apportioned and includes benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge. It remains unchanged by wider action, poverty, or retirement, rooted in the heart and unfolding outward as harmony, fullness, and character in the limbs.

is_rooted_in the superior man's nature [in the heart] Propriety is one of the qualities belonging by nature to the superior man. It is rooted in his heart and contributes to its outward manifestation throughout his body.

is_rooted_in the superior man's nature [in the heart] Knowledge is one of the qualities belonging by nature to the superior man. It is rooted in his heart and contributes to its outward manifestation throughout his body.

l: Bo Yi, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Bo Yi avoids Zhou while dwelling on the northern sea coast, then hears of king Wen’s rise and decides to follow him, valuing the chief of the West’s care for the old.

l: Tai Gong Wang, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Tai Gong avoids Zhou while dwelling on the eastern sea coast, then hears of king Wen’s rise and chooses to follow him, valuing the chief of the West’s care for the old.

l: a prince (the kingdom's hypothetical prince), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: A kingdom’s prince nourishes old people well, regulating land and households, teaching cultivation and animal raising, and attracting virtuous men.

l: old people, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Old people were to receive silk and flesh; by fifty silk maintained warmth, and by seventy flesh satisfied appetite.

l: all men of virtue, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: gather_to a prince (the kingdom's hypothetical prince) [as the proper object] All men of virtue would feel that a prince who knew well how to nourish the old was the proper object for them to gather to.

l: each family, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Each family keeps five brood hens and two brood sows through breeding seasons so the old can eat flesh.

l: the people of king Wen, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: have no aged who were starved or famished The people of king Wen had no aged people who were starved or famished.
Food, used seasonably by the people, came from brood-hen and brood-sow families and 100-mu farms, securing eight-mouth families against want.

l: the rise of king Wen, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The rise of king Wen prompted Bo Yi and Tai Gong to decide to follow him after they heard that the chief of the West knew well how to nourish the old.

l: nourishing the old, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Nourishing the old involved regulating fields and dwellings, planting mulberry trees, raising animals, and instructing wives and children to care for their aged. It provided the old with silk to wear and flesh to eat.

l: starvation and famine, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: describe persons not kept warm nor supplied with food Persons who were not kept warm or supplied with food were described as starved and famished. Among the people of king Wen, no aged people suffered this condition.
is_abundant abundant [as water and fire under sage governance] Grain should be abundant under good governance, as abundant as water and fire. Its abundance is connected with the people's virtue.
is_light light [on the people] Taxes should be made light so the people may become rich.

l: prescribed ceremonies, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The prescribed ceremonies are the proper objects on which the people should expend their wealth.
Water is necessary for the people’s life and so abundant that anyone requesting it at dusk receives it.
Fire is necessary for the people’s life, abundant among them, and given by man when requested at dusk.
governs kingdom [so as to make pulse and grain abundant] A sage governs the kingdom so that pulse and grain are as abundant as water and fire.

Confucius is a sage whose doctrines, received through transmission from king Wen and earlier sages, were passed to later generations. He seeks scholars pursuing the true medium, but when they cannot be found turns to the ardent and cautiously-decided, while judging careful village people thieves of virtue. Leaving Lu gradually and Qi abruptly, he suffers from unsympathetic rulers and ministers. Ascending hills and the Tai mountain makes Lu, then all beneath the heavens, seem small.
Lu appeared small to Confucius after he ascended the eastern hill.

l: Tai mountain, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Confucius ascended the Tai mountain, after which all beneath the heavens appeared small to him.
makes_other_waters_difficult_to_contemplate other waters A person who has contemplated the sea finds it difficult to think anything of other waters.

l: gate of the sage, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: makes_words_difficult_to_contemplate words of others [for one who has wandered in it] A person who has wandered in the gate of the sage finds it difficult to think anything of the words of others.
has gate of the sage The sage is associated with a gate whose teachings make other people’s words difficult to value in comparison.
Water, contemplated as foaming waves, flows through its course only after filling the hollows it encounters.
Student sets mind on the sage's doctrines and advances toward them by completing lessons one after another.

l: the doctrines of the sages, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The doctrines of the sages pass through successive generations, from Yao and Shun through Tang, king Wen, and Confucius. Students approach them gradually by completing lessons, while the text asks whether anyone remains to transmit them further.
has_disciple disciple of Zhi Zhi is associated with the person who rises at cock-crowing and addresses himself earnestly to the pursuit of gain.
Gain is something a person may earnestly pursue after rising at cock-crowing. Its thought is contrasted with the thought of virtue.

l: interval between gain and virtue, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: An interval between thoughts of gain and virtue separates Shun from Zhi, reciprocally distinguishing each from the other.
Yang is a philosopher who holds that each person should act for himself, refusing even a single-hair sacrifice to benefit the kingdom.
Mo is a philosopher who loves all equally and would rub smooth his whole body to benefit the kingdom.

l: Zi Mo, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Zi Mo holds a medium between Yang and Mo, nearer the right, but rigid adherence leaves no room for changing circumstances.

l: Each one for himself, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Each one for himself is the principle attributed to Yang. It means that each person acts for himself rather than making a personal sacrifice for the kingdom.

l: the true medium, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The medium, Zi Mo’s position between Yang and Mo, lies nearer the right; without room for changing circumstances, it hardens into harmful rigidity.

l: right principles, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Right principle is harmed by rigidly holding one point while ignoring many circumstances. Its presence throughout the kingdom coincides with a person's principles appearing with that person; when it disappears, both the principles and person vanish. Its manifestation does not depend on other men.
Hunger makes food seem sweet, and when severe injures the palate and mind.
Thirst makes any drink seem rightly sweet, yet when severe injures the palate and can injure the mind.

l: mind (men's minds), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Men's minds are injured by hunger and thirst; preventing these harms removes reason to sorrow about inequality with other men.

l: Hui of Liu Xia, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Hui of Liu Xia is of Liu Xia, maintains a firm purpose of life, and would not change it for three highest offices.

l: firm purpose of life, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Hui of Liu Xia would not have changed his firm purpose of life for the three highest offices of State.

l: man with definite aims to be accomplished, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: A man with definite aims is compared to a well-digger: stopping before reaching the spring throws away his effort.
A well with a spring is dug seventy-two cubits, then abandoned before reaching it, wasting the effort.

l: benevolence and righteousness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Benevolence and righteousness were natural to Yao and Shun, adopted by Tang and Wu, and feigned by five chiefs.
Yao naturally had benevolence and righteousness, earnestly loved the virtuous, and focused his limited wisdom on what mattered.
makes_own benevolence and righteousness Tang made benevolence and righteousness his own.
makes_own benevolence and righteousness Wu made benevolence and righteousness his own.

l: five chiefs of the princes, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Five chiefs of the princes feign and borrow benevolence and righteousness for a long time, never returning them and obscuring that they do not own them.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Gong Sun Chou is a questioner of Mencius. He asks about worthy ministers banishing unvirtuous sovereigns, superior men eating without labour, mourning and a king’s son, and whether lofty principles should be made more attainable to encourage daily effort.

l: Yi Yin, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Yi Yin, a minister, banishes disobedient Tai Jia to Tong, then brings him back after he becomes virtuous.

l: Tai Jia, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Tai Jia is banished to Tong by Yi Yin for disobedience, becomes virtuous, and is brought back.
Mencius teaches that sharing Yi Yin’s purpose determines whether a minister’s banishment of a sovereign is permissible.
Mencius says that banishing a sovereign without the same purpose as Yi Yin would be usurpation.

A country gains tranquillity, wealth, and glory when its sovereign employs a superior man’s counsels; following his instructions, its young become filial, obedient to elders, true-hearted, and faithful.

l: bread of idleness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The bread of idleness is presented as something the Book of Poetry says a person should not eat.
Dian, a king's son, asks Mencius about an unemployed scholar’s business and exalting the aim; after his mother’s death, he seeks mourning but cannot complete the full period.

l: unemployed scholar, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: has_business exalting his aim The unemployed scholar should exalt his aim by committing himself simply to benevolence and righteousness.
The aim becomes exalted by being set simply on benevolence and righteousness.

l: great man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: has_business complete [when benevolence is the dwelling-place of the heart and righteousness the path of life] The great man has completed his business when benevolence is the dwelling-place of the heart and righteousness is the path of life.
is_a complete business of a great man The business of the unemployed scholar is to exalt his aim, while the business of a great man is complete when he lives with benevolence and righteousness.

l: kingdom of Qi, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: is_offered_to Chen Zhong [contrary to righteousness] The kingdom of Qi is imagined as being offered to Chen Zhong contrary to righteousness. Chen Zhong would not receive it.

l: Chen Zhong, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: does_not_receive kingdom of Qi [when offered contrary to righteousness] Chen Zhong would refuse the kingdom of Qi if it were offered contrary to righteousness. People regard him as a man of the highest worth because he would decline a dish of rice or a plate of soup.

l: parents and relatives, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Disowning parents and relatives is described as one of the greatest crimes a man can commit.

l: greatest crimes, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Greatest crimes are defined as disowning parents and relatives and rejecting sovereign-minister and superior-inferior relations.

l: relation of sovereign and minister, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The relation of sovereign and minister is identified as an important relation that must not be rejected. Rejecting it is described as a greater crime than declining a dish of rice or a plate of soup.

l: relation of superiors and inferiors, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The relation of superiors and inferiors is identified as an important relation that must not be rejected. Rejecting it is described as a greater crime than declining a dish of rice or a plate of soup.

l: great excellences, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: are_not_credited_for small excellence [because a man possesses it] Great excellences should not be credited to a man merely because he possesses a small excellence. Mencius uses Chen Zhong's small act of righteousness to illustrate this point.

l: Gao Yao, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Gao Yao, chief minister of justice, receives proper law and would apprehend Gu Sou for murder.

l: Gu Sou, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Gu Sou is presented in a hypothetical case as having murdered a man. Shun would privately carry him into concealment and live with him along the sea-coast.

l: murder of a man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The hypothetical murder of a man by Gu Sou would lead Gao Yao to apprehend him.
The law had been received by Gao Yao from a proper source.
Qi was the destination of Mencius's journey from Fan. The king of Qi's son was present there.

l: king Xuan of Qi, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: King Xuan of Qi is a king whose residence, carriages, horses, and dress resemble other men’s, while his distinctive air and appearance arise from his peculiar position in the wide house of the world. He has a son and later wants to shorten mourning.

alters air [as nurture affects the body] Position alters a person's air and can make someone look different even when his residence, carriages and horses, and dress resemble those of other men. Corresponding positions also accounted for the prince of Lu's voice resembling that of their prince.
Air is altered by a person's position, just as nurture affects the body. A peculiar air should distinguish someone whose position is in the wide house of the world.

l: prince of Lu, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: When the prince of Lu went to Song, he called out at the Die Shi gate. The gatekeeper recognized that his voice closely resembled that of their prince because of the correspondence of their positions.

l: influence of position, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: is_a influence [great] The influence of position is described as great. It changes a person's air and appearance and can produce a similarity in voice between people holding corresponding positions.

l: Mencius's journey from Fan to Qi, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Mencius journeys from Fan to Qi, sees the king of Qi’s son, and reflects on position’s effect.
A scholar is compared to a pig when fed without love and a domestic animal when loved without respect.

l: honouring and respecting, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: exists_before offering of gifts [before any offering] Honouring and respecting exist before any offering of gifts. When they lack genuine reality, empty demonstrations of them are insufficient.

l: man (Mencius's man), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: A man can satisfy the design of his bodily organization only after becoming a sage.

l: bodily organs, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: belong_to Heaven-conferred nature [with their functions] The bodily organs have functions that belong to Heaven-conferred nature.
Mourning for one whole year was presented as better than eliminating it. When completing the whole period was impossible, even adding a single day was considered better than not mourning at all.

is_effected_by the superior man Teaching is effected through five methods: seasonable influence, perfecting virtue, assisting talents, answering inquiries, and encouraging self-cultivation and correction.

l: five ways of teaching, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: is_a methods [for effecting teaching] The five ways are the superior man's influence descending like seasonable rain, perfecting virtue, assisting the development of talents, answering inquiries, and privately cultivating and correcting oneself.
Gong Sun Chou describes principles as lofty and admirable, yet difficult to attain.
Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius to adapt his teaching so that learners will consider the principles attainable and exert themselves daily.

l: person (the individual whose principles are discussed), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: A person whose presence depends on right principles prevailing throughout the kingdom, vanishing with those principles when they disappear.

l: Gong Du, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: is_a disciple Gong Du asks Mencius why he did not answer Geng of Tang when Geng of Tang appeared in Mencius's school.

l: Geng of Tang, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Geng of Tang appears in Mencius's school, where Mencius declines to answer because of two presumptions.

l: the superior man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The superior man distinguishes his relations: kind but not loving to inferior creatures, loving but not affectionate to people generally, and affectionate to parents. He cultivates himself, follows righteousness without seeking reward, rejects treating natural pleasures as his nature or moral conduct as fate, despises rulers’ pomp, and seeks to restore an unchanging standard.

l: inferior creatures, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Inferior creatures receive kindness from the superior man, but not love.

l: people generally, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: People generally receive love and a loving disposition from the superior man, but not affection.
The superior man is affectionate to his parents.

l: the wise, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The wise embrace all knowledge, while being most earnest about what is of greatest importance.

l: what is of the greatest importance, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: What is of the greatest importance is the proper focus of earnest attention for the wise and the benevolent.

l: the benevolent, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The benevolent embrace all in love, while most earnestly cultivating affection for the virtuous.

l: the virtuous, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: The virtuous are the proper objects of the benevolent's earnest affection.
Yao and Shun’s wisdom did not extend to everything, unfolding through earnest attention to what was important.

l: the three years' mourning, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: is_kept by a person [not able to keep it] The three years' mourning is presented as something a person may be unable to keep, while being very particular about shorter mourning periods.

l: ignorance of what is most important, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Ignorance of what is most important is shown by failing the three years’ mourning, focusing on details of shorter mourning periods, eating and swilling soup immoderately, and asking about not tearing meat with the teeth.

l: the sovereign, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: is_a the lightest [among the people, the spirits of the land and grain, and the sovereign] The sovereign is considered less important than the people and the spirits of the land and grain. To become sovereign, one must gain the peasantry, and a sovereign who endangers the altars may be replaced.

Scholars face laughter and suffering from men when returning to former occupations. Mencius distinguishes ambitious and cautiously-decided scholars from village people, whom Confucius called thieves of virtue.

l: a sage, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: A sage is a teacher whose example across a hundred generations reforms corrupt, weak, mean, and niggardly people; sages’ doctrines pass from Yao and Shun through Tang, king Wen, and Confucius, and may culminate beyond ordinary knowledge as a spirit-man.

requires the great principles of government [and their various business] Government and its business are among the precious things of a prince, and without their great principles there will not be enough wealth for expenditure. Proper government requires rules of propriety, distinctions of right, and the trust placed in men of virtue and ability.
War is a ruler’s claimed skill and a great crime; Mencius says no Spring and Autumn war is righteous, as hostile States cannot correct one another and benevolence surpasses warfare.
Desires for bodily pleasures are natural, but Mencius says few desires best nourish the mind; many desires make keeping the heart difficult.

l: natural human feelings, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin)
s: Natural human feelings include desire for pleasure and ease, aversion to injuring others, and reluctance toward wrongs; extending what one cannot bear or will not do into action produces benevolence and righteousness.
